author: A Robot
objectives: Students will determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Students will predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Students will distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Students will explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Students will apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Introduces the fundamental concept of VSEPR theory: electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize mutual repulsion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand that electron pairs repel each other.
Recognize that molecular geometry is determined by the arrangement of electron domains.
instructions: Observe the central atom and the Lewis structure of water.
Listen to the narration to understand the basic principle of VSEPR theory.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the VSEPR theory title and a brief description.
clips.narration: Welcome to the VSEPR theory lab. VSEPR stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion. This theory helps us predict the three-dimensional geometry of covalent molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: Show a central atom and a reference Lewis structure for water.
clips.narration: The core idea of VSEPR is simple: electron pairs around a central atom repel each other. To minimize this repulsion, these electron domains arrange themselves as far apart as possible in three-dimensional space. We start with a flat Lewis structure, like this one for water, and use it to determine the number of electron domains - both bonding pairs and lone pairs - around the central atom.
